blocks.text: Non-comparison sorting algorithms do NOT compare elements against each other. Instead they use the actual values, digits, or structure of the data to sort. This lets them break the O(n log n) barrier that all comparison sorts are bound by.
The key idea: Instead of asking "is A greater than B?", these algorithms ask "what digit does A have in the tens place?" or "how many times does each value appear?" completely different thinking.

content.title: 1. Why Can We Beat O(n log n)?

blocks.text: Comparison sorts are limited because each comparison only gives 1 bit of information (yes/no). Non-comparison sorts extract more information per step by looking at the actual value of elements.
1. Comparison sort
Each step: "Is A > B?" yes or no.
One bit of info. Needs at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons total. Can't go below O(n log n).
2. Non-comparison sort
Each step: "What is the value of A?" extracts many bits at once. Doesn't reduce possibilities one-by-one. Can achieve O(n) with right constraints.

The catch: Non-comparison sorts only work under specific conditions usually integers within a known range. They don't work on arbitrary data like strings, floats, or custom objects without special handling.
The simplest non-comparison sort. Count how many times each value appears, then reconstruct the sorted array from those counts.
Core idea: If I know value 3 appears twice and value 5 appears three times, I can place them directly in sorted order without ever comparing them to each other.
Step-by-Step Example
Sort: [4, 2, 2, 8, 3, 3, 1] values range from 0 to 8
Phase 1: Count occurrences of each value
count[ ]: index = value, value = how many times it appears:
Phase 2: Rebuild output from count array
Walk through the count array left to right. For each index i with count[i] = k, write the value i exactly k times into the output.
Rebuild output: read count array L→R, write each value count[i] times:
Sorted! No comparisons made at any point.

items: Time: O(n + k) where n = number of elements, k = range of values (max - min + 1)
Space: O(n + k): needs count array of size k and output array of size n
Stable? Yes: with the cumulative count version (see below)
Constraint: Only works on non-negative integers. Range k must be small relative to n.

blocks.text: When does it fail? If you have n=100 elements but values range from 0 to 1,000,000, the count array needs 1 million slots. k dominates and you'd use more memory and time than a comparison sort.

The simple version above loses stability (it just re-writes values). The stable version uses cumulative counts to place each element in its exact final position.
Sort numbers digit by digit from the least significant digit (ones) to the most significant digit. Uses a stable sort (usually Counting Sort) at each digit level.

Core idea: If you sort by ones first, then by tens (stably), then by hundreds (stably) after the last pass the array is fully sorted. Stability at each pass is critical it preserves the ordering from previous passes.
Step-by-Step Example
Radix Sort sorts numbers digit by digit, starting from the least significant digit (ones place)and moving left to tens, hundreds, etc.It uses astable sort(usually Counting Sort) at each digit.

Final Sorted Array
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

When sorting by the tens digit, the ordering based on the ones digit is preserved because the intermediate sort is stable. Similarly, when sorting by the hundreds digit, the ordering based on the tens and ones digits remains intact.
By processing digits from right to left and preserving previous orderings, the entire array becomes sorted after the most significant digit is processed.
One-Line Intuition
Radix Sort sorts numbers one digit at a time (ones → tens → hundreds), and stability ensures that information from previous passes is never lost.

Why LSD (Least Significant Digit first)? Because the last sort (most significant digit) takes highest priority. Each previous sort's result is preserved by stability, so everything falls into place after the final pass.

items: Time: O(n × k) where n = elements, k = number of digits in max value
Space: O(n + b) where b = base (10 for decimal)
Stable?: Yes because each digit-level sort uses stable Counting Sort
Constraint: Works on integers or fixed-length strings. Number of digits k must be small.

blocks.text: Distribute elements into a number of buckets, sort each bucket individually (usually with Insertion Sort), then concatenate all buckets.

Core idea: If we know data is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, we can create n buckets each covering a range like [0, 0.1), [0.1, 0.2)... Elements in each bucket are close to each other, so each bucket has very few elements and sorts fast.
Step-by-Step Example

Bucket Sort works by dividing the input range into several buckets. Numbers are first placed into their appropriate buckets, then each bucket is sorted individually, and finally all buckets are combined to produce the sorted array.
Step 1: Distribute Elements into Buckets
The range [0, 1) is divided into buckets:
Place each number into its corresponding bucket:
At this stage, numbers are only grouped by range and are not necessarily sorted within each bucket.
Step 2: Sort Each Bucket Individually
Each bucket is sorted separately, usually using Insertion Sort because buckets are typically small.
Now every bucket contains elements in sorted order.
Step 3: Concatenate the Buckets
Combine the buckets from left to right:
Final sorted array:
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
Bucket Sort works because numbers that belong to a smaller range are placed into the same bucket.
Since all elements in an earlier bucket are smaller than every element in a later bucket, sorting individual buckets and then joining them automatically produces a globally sorted array.
One-Line Intuition
Bucket Sort distributes elements into range-based buckets, sorts each bucket separately, and then merges the buckets to obtain the final sorted order.

items: Time (avg): O(n + k) when data is uniformly distributed each bucket has ~1 element
Time (worst): O(n²) if all elements land in one bucket degrades to insertion sort
Space: O(n + k) for n elements across k buckets
Best for: Uniformly distributed floating-point numbersin a known range

items: Use Counting Sort: when Sorting integers with a small, known range. Example: student grades (0–100), ages (0–120), dice rolls (1–6).
Use Radix Sort: when Sorting large integers or fixed-length strings. Example: phone numbers, ZIP codes, employee IDs. Number of digits d is small.
Use Bucket Sort: when Data is floating-point and roughly uniformly distributed. Example: sensor readings between 0 and 1, normalised scores.
Stick to comparison sort: when Data has no special structure arbitrary strings, custom objects, mixed types. Merge Sort or Timsort is the right choice.

blocks.text: Real-world example: Sorting 10 million phone numbers (10 digits each).
Radix Sort does 10 passes over 10M elements = 100M operations. Merge Sort does 10M × log(10M) ≈ 230M operations. Radix Sort is 2× faster here a meaningful gain at scale.
Non-comparison sorts live to the right of the O(n log n) wall but only under specific conditions
